newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov gets new budget pact, almost 4 months late.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov gets new budget pact, almost 4 months late.

text.p: New York State Governor George Pataki Tuesday said he reached a fiscal 1998 budget pact with the legislature that would cut property taxes by $2.2 billion and eventually end some clothing sales taxes.
The $67 billion agreement, which still must be finally approved, would set aside $530 million for a reserve fund.
New York State's budget was due on April 1, and this year it surpassed last year's new national record for late budgets, when it did not agree a new plan until July 13.
Pataki said the new budget pact would raise General Fund Spending to $34.5 billion, saying spending had risen a mere 0.9 percent each year in the three budgets he has approved.

"That is the lowest three-year average increase in spending in state history and well under the rate of inflation over three years," he said, in a statement. He added that when he was elected two years ago, the state had a $5 billion deficit.

The Republican governor added state aid for schools would rise $750 million, which he said was the biggest increase in New York State's history. He added changes to the welfare system would require recipients to work, while more money would be spent on child care and job training.

The School Tax Relief plan, which would start in 1998 and be fully implemented in 2002, would cut property taxes on homeowners, condominium and cooperative owners by an average of 27 percent, with seniors seeing rates fall 45 percent.

New York City's personal income tax cut would drop 10 percent by the time a cut was fully implemented in 2001. The phase-out, which would start in 1998, would supplement the city's school property tax savings and give it another $464 million to ensure the school tax relief plan was equitable.

The state's share of clothing sales taxes on items that cost less than $100--except for footwear--would be eliminated in fiscal 1999. In fiscal 1998, clothing buyers would get the same two, one-week moratoriums in January and September they got last year on items of clothing that cost $500 or less.

The Gross Receipts Tax on energy and telecommunications would be cut by nearly 30 percent to 2.5 percent. The phased-in reduction would start in 1998 and be fully effective in 2000, when it would save $400 million. And the petroleum business tax paid by trucking and railroad companies would be cut by nearly two cents per gallon over the next three years from 13.74 cents per gallon.
Pataki also won agreement to build one maximum security prison, with 750 cells, as part of an expansion program that would add a total of 1,550 cells.
Gradually eliminating taxes on the healthcare industry wuld save them more than $530 million in 1997, he added.

"By continuing to cut taxes on senior citizens and middle-class families, by replacing the failed old welfare system with a new system of hope and opportunity, by keeping violent felons in prison where they no longer threaten our people, by making historic investments in education and environment, we are creating safer and more prosperous state for all New Yorkers," Pataki said, in prepared remarks.
